Warcraft III is a real-time strategy game from 2002. You gather gold and lumber, build a base, research technology, raise heroes and an army, and destroy your opponent while they do the same. More than twenty years on, people still play it competitively, and streamers such as former pro player Grubby and the casters of Back2Warcraft bring it to large audiences.

This post is about an agent that plays the whole game of Warcraft III on the classic ladder map Echo Isles , under the game’s own rules, against the strongest opponent the game ships with, the built-in AI on insane , the hardest of its levels (easy, normal and insane). It now wins about nine games in ten. Here is how it got there.

## Why this is hard

Most games last 10 to 25 minutes, with thousands of decisions for dozens of units at once. There are four races, human, orc, undead and night elf, each with its own units, buildings and spells, and a fog of war hides the opponent. The one real reward, a win or a loss, comes at the very end. DeepMind’s AlphaStar (StarCraft II) and OpenAI Five (Dota 2) mastered games like this in 2019 and beat top human players, with the game makers’ help and a datacenter. AlphaStar trained 12 agents for 44 days on 32 TPUs each. I had one desktop and a game that was never built for any of this.

## Running the real game, fast

Warcraft III has no API for bots, no headless mode and no faster-than-real-time option. It is a 32-bit Windows program, and its rules, pathfinding, spells and AI hold so many details that reimplementing them faithfully would be very hard. So I run the real thing, under Wine on Linux, about 50 copies at once, and drive it from Python.

The harness , written in the game’s own map-scripting language, reports what the player can see every half second of game time and carries out the agent’s orders. The shim , a small DLL inside the game process, replaces the game’s clocks with a virtual one, so the game runs as fast as the CPU allows and waits at every step for Python’s orders. Games are deterministic, so a replay reproduces a game step for step. That is how every video here was made.

Self-play speed, agent steps per second

An agent step is one decision by one player, made every half second of game time. Each bar adds one optimization to the ones above it.

Most of the speed came from removing waste, not from adding hardware. The games skip drawing, five games share one map load, the per-unit bookkeeping moved from the game’s script into C, and the network runs as CUDA graphs from a C++ loop. Today the desktop plays about 50 games at once, each about 15 times faster than real time, which adds up to roughly 730 hours of Warcraft III every hour .

## The agent

Swipe sideways to see the whole diagram →

The agent sees only what its player sees, and every half second it decides for every one of its units at once. The network has four main parts:

- The order head picks each unit’s order, such as train, build, attack, move, cast or nothing.

- The target heads pick what that order is aimed at, either a unit in view or a point on the map. A point is picked as x and then y, so both coordinates belong to the same spot.

- The memory carries a state from step to step, so the agent can remember what it saw before it went out of view.

- The value head predicts how the game will end. It reads hidden information and is only used in training.

The whole network is small, about 3.2 million weights. One decision for 60 units, with 120 in view, takes about 13 milliseconds on four cores of an ordinary CPU, far less than the half second it has.

A head start from the built-in AI. Learning by playing from scratch is too hard: an agent that gives random orders almost never wins, so it has nothing to learn from. To give it a good start, I recorded thousands of games of the built-in AI playing itself and trained the agent to copy the orders the AI gave. This is called behavioral cloning , and it leaves the agent playing roughly like the AI.

Learning from playing. Once the copying stops improving, the agent switches to self-play. It plays against a league of opponents (itself, its past selves and the built-in AI) and learns from the reward. The reward is +1 for a win and −1 for a loss, plus small rewards along the way for gaining material (more on those later). After each batch of games, every order the agent gave is judged by the reward that followed it, using policy gradients . If the reward turned out better than the value head expected at that moment, the order becomes a little more likely in that situation; if worse, a little less. The gap between the reward and what was expected is called the advantage .

Keeping it steady. A second term, a KL divergence , pulls the agent back towards an earlier version of itself, the anchor , so one noisy batch cannot undo what already works.

## Measuring progress

Training numbers can’t tell whether a change made the agent better. The reward includes the small material rewards, not just wins and losses, and the training opponents change all the time, from past versions of the agent to a built-in AI that is made easier or harder as the agent improves. So every training run also plays test games that it never learns from. They are games against the built-in AI at the hardest level each stage aims at, without any tax or other help for the agent. On the real map that is insane. Each experiment is a new run that starts from the best agent so far, with one change. The new version and the one it started from play exactly the same matchups, with the same races and sides, so their win rates can be compared directly. A few hundred games each are enough to see clear differences. Every experiment, with its numbers, is in the experiment log .

## How it learned

The problem. A real game often lasts 25 minutes, and the agent decides twice a second, for all of its units at once. That is 25 × 60 × 2, about 3,000 decisions per side before the one reward, a win or a loss, arrives. With a single result at the end it is hard to tell which of those decisions mattered, and an agent that loses every game gets nothing to learn from. Even an agent trained by behavioral cloning on the built-in AI’s games on the real map lost all 40 of its test games.

A curriculum. So the training follows a curriculum: the agent starts with easier problems and moves on to harder ones as it gets better. It began with small fights, then whole games on a small map with sped-up rules, then longer games, then the real map, first with fast rules and then with the game’s own. At each stage the test games showed a problem, experiments went after it, and most of them failed. These are the ones that worked, in the order they came.

The first stage was small fights: a hero and a few units on each side, over in seconds. This is where the basics were worked out, such as units as tokens, targets as pointers, starting from behavioral cloning of a scripted player, and a league of past selves.

### 27 September – 2 October Two-minute games

The first whole games were played on a small flat duel map with two bases laid out like Echo Isles’ main bases, with the rules sped up seven times, so a game took two minutes. The agent began with behavioral cloning of the built-in AI’s orders. On its first day of self-play it lost game after game, even against the easy AI.

#### A fair opponent

What was wrong. The first self-play run lost all of its last 75 games against the AI, so it had nothing to learn from. Two ways of making the AI easier failed, because the agent exploited both. With extra hit points for its units, it never learned to spend its money. Against an AI that started late, it simply rushed the AI before it could do anything.

The change. A tax on the AI. It plays normally, but loses a share of the gold and lumber it gathers. The share grows after each of the agent’s losses and shrinks after each win, so the agent wins about half of those games. The test games never have a tax.

The outcome. As the agent improved, the tax fell from about 75% to almost zero, averaged over all matchups. By 2 October it won 79% of its test games against the AI.

### 2 – 14 October Six-minute games, against insane

The next stage had slower rules and a harder opponent, the built-in AI on insane. Against the untaxed AI, games took about six minutes. The agent again started from behavioral cloning, this time of the AI’s games under these rules. The tax kept the training games balanced, but they didn’t teach much. Most of the taxed training games dragged on and ended in a tie at the 20-minute time limit. The agent built more than the taxed AI, but sat on about 4,000 gold and lumber it never spent, and hardly attacked. The tax also hid how slowly the agent started. One minute in, the taxed AI had 7 supply against the agent’s 15, but the untaxed AI had 21 and won the test games in five to seven minutes.

#### On-policy distillation from the built-in AI

What was wrong. After hours of self-play the agent had won only 1 of 98 test games. Behavioral cloning only shows the agent situations that the built-in AI itself gets into. The built-in AI always keeps its buildings busy, so its games almost never show an idle barracks with money to spend, and the agent never learned what to do there.

The change. Let the built-in AI coach the agent in half of its training games. The built-in AI watches the agent’s game. In every situation the agent gets into, the built-in AI notes the order it would give, and training nudges the agent’s orders towards those notes. This is on-policy distillation .

The outcome. Within fifty minutes of training the agent went from 1 win in 98 test games to 13 in 50, and the training games stopped ending in ties.

Over the next week and a half, most experiments made no difference. Two did.

#### Credit that skips mistakes

What was wrong. A game’s result is spread back over every action before it, so a good move followed by a lost fight was blamed for the fight.

The change. Switch to AlphaStar’s UPGO. With it, a move gets credit from what actually happened next only until the first later move that went worse than expected. After that point, it is judged by what the value head expected instead.

The outcome. Over two runs, this was the largest gain on the six-minute map.

#### Stop on-policy distillation

What was wrong. The agent now won about 60% of its games against insane, so it had become better than the built-in AI coaching it. Yet copying the built-in AI’s orders still made up most of each training update.

The change. Stop on-policy distillation.

The outcome. It won more often against insane, and training ran faster without the built-in AI coaching in the games.

### 15 – 17 October The real map

By 14 October the agent won 80% of its games against insane on the six-minute map, so it moved on to the real map, Echo Isles. The real map is far bigger and busier than the duel map, and a few things had to change for it:

- Where things are. Positions are now measured from the agent’s own base, at the scale it knew from the duel map, and the stretch between the bases is squeezed so that the enemy base is where it expects it. Without that, its buildings landed in the trees and its attacks went to the middle of the map, where the enemy base used to be.

- Where it can point. The grid of map points it can target grew from 128 to 352 cells a side, to cover the bigger map.

- The rules, in two steps. Training first used Echo Isles with the fast rules of the six-minute games, then the game’s own rules.

The agent was trained on Echo Isles with the fast rules only. Tested under the game’s real rules, which it had never played, it won 49% straight away. From there it kept improving:
